# Evaluating the AI Architect {#sec-evaluating-agentic-architect}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"Measurement is the first step that leads to control and eventually to improvement. If you can’t measure something, you can’t understand it. If you can’t understand it, you can’t control it. If you can’t control it, you can’t improve it."*
>
> — H. James Harrington, *Business Process Improvement* (1991) [@Harrington1991BusinessProcess]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** H. James Harrington, an author and quality engineer, emphasized that systemic improvement requires rigorous, well-defined measurement. In AI-assisted hardware design, the immediate temptation is to measure the final instructions-per-cycle (IPC) of the generated chip. But this conflates a lucky guess with systemic engineering capability. To build reliable systems, we must measure the *agent*, not just the *artifact*.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
How do we measure the AI architect rather than the artifact it produced, so that a score reflects a search under real physical constraints, survives contamination, prices what the search cost, and converts into a defensible grant of autonomy?
:::

@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack scaled the loop across the full hardware stack. But once that loop is running at any level, the architect must evaluate its efficiency. With two different agents optimizing the same low-power RISC-V XR subsystem, how do we decide which one to trust?

In a traditional workflow, evaluation focuses on the artifact. Does the final compiled netlist meet the timing and power budget? When evaluating agents, judging the artifact alone is not enough. An agent might stumble onto a valid configuration through brute force, running tens of thousands of failed EDA simulations before getting lucky. The final artifact might pass, but the process that produced it is inefficient and economically unviable.

Evaluating the agent rather than the artifact requires measuring the search trajectory itself, ensuring the resulting score can be trusted against benchmark contamination, and turning that score into an actionable decision. The three build on each other, because a metric is only as useful as the benchmark that produces it, and a benchmark is only useful if it dictates how much autonomy the architect grants the agent.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Reject a reported design gain that does not name the RTL, process design kit, constraints, tool version, and signoff corner behind it.
- Refuse to compare two agent scores until each names its model, its harness, and its budget, because a comparison across harnesses ranks engineering teams rather than models.
- Demand a random-search null baseline at the same budget before crediting a trajectory score as reasoning, and require the margin to clear the apparatus's own noise floor rather than merely look convincing.
- Separate a metric that is specified from one that is only named, and state the convention behind any score you report.
- Aggregate across a suite with the geometric mean of normalized ratios, never the arithmetic mean, and match an agent's autonomy to the evidence level its results reached, reserving the waiver, the right to change the checks, and the commitment boundary for people.
:::

## From Artifact Metrics to Trajectory Metrics

Before we can benchmark an AI architect, we should recall why human architects measure anything at all. Computer architecture is a strictly empirical discipline. Architects do not evaluate a processor by reading its source code; they evaluate it by running standardized workloads such as SPEC CPU, a standard suite of compute-intensive integer and floating-point programs, or MLPerf, an industry-standard machine learning benchmark, and measuring the physical consequences, including IPC, power, area, and latency.

Historically, benchmarks have served as the foundational bedrock for both computer architecture and machine learning as independent fields. Computer architects rely on SPEC to measure core compute throughput and on PARSEC, a multi-threaded workload suite, to measure shared-memory parallel scaling, while machine learning researchers rely on ImageNet, a standard computer vision dataset, and SWE-bench to evaluate model generalization. However, evaluating the AI architect requires benchmarks that exist precisely at the intersection of these two areas. Constructing these intersectional benchmarks demands deep domain expertise from both disciplines: the machine learning expertise to rigorously measure model variance and data contamination, coupled with the architecture expertise to measure cycle-accurate physical consequences and EDA tool telemetry. As introduced in @sec-moonshot, this cross-disciplinary reality changes the definition of success.

Because building a physical chip costs millions of dollars and takes years [@Shilov2023IBSDesignCost], architects measure these properties early and often using simulators and analytical models such as the Roofline model [@Williams2009Roofline] or McPAT [@McPAT]. The goal of traditional architectural measurement is risk reduction. Each measurement buys confidence that a design point will meet its physical requirements before the team commits it to silicon.

When an agent enters the loop, the object of measurement shifts. As established, evaluating the artifact alone hides whether the search reached the design through methodical reasoning or brute force. This distinction matters because an unreasoned search does not *transfer*. An agent that finds a five percent gain by luck cannot explain which change caused it, cannot reproduce the result on the next workload, and cannot be trusted to know when to stop.

In hardware, this lack of causality carries a steep penalty. In software, a stochastic search that eventually types a working script wastes ten milliseconds per try. In architecture, a search that burns ten thousand hours of EDA tool licenses and compute-cluster core-hours to find a gain destroys tape-out schedules. So the evaluator measures the *trajectory* of design as a proxy for two things a single final score hides. The first is whether a result will survive physical synthesis. The second is whether the agent can safely be given more autonomy. That reframing, from Human-Labor-Dominated NRE[^fn-nre-c10] to Compute-Dominated NRE, changes what each evaluation dimension measures (@tbl-eval-shift).

| **Dimension** | **Evaluating the Artifact (Traditional)** | **Evaluating the Agent (Architecture 2.0)** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What is measured? | The physical consequences of the processor. | The algorithmic efficiency of the search under physical constraints. |
| Benchmark suites | SPEC CPU, MLPerf, PARSEC [@PARSEC]. | ArchEval [@WangEtAl2026ArchEval], VerilogEval [@VerilogEval], RTLLM [@RTLLM]. |
| Primary Cost | Human salaries and schedule months (Labor-Dominated NRE). | Scalable compute and licensing (Compute-Dominated NRE). |
| Failure Mode | Thermal throttling, timing violations. | Unroutable netlists, PDN violations, ignored formal equivalence constraints. |
| Goal of Measurement | Prove the chip works. | Prove the agent can reason causally about hardware constraints. |

: **From measuring the chip to measuring the agent:** Evaluating an AI architect requires a different set of metrics than evaluating the chip it produces. {#tbl-eval-shift tbl-colwidths="[20,40,40]"}

The three suites in the right-hand column are worth distinguishing, because they are the closest prior art to what this chapter argues is missing. VerilogEval scores whether a model can turn a natural-language specification into functionally correct Verilog, checking the result against a testbench [@VerilogEval]. RTLLM does the same at design scale, adding syntax and functional goals alongside a rough quality measure [@RTLLM]. ArchEval reaches furthest toward physical constraints [@WangEtAl2026ArchEval]. What none of them scores is the trajectory: how much compute and EDA time the search consumed, whether the agent reasoned about the physical constraint or stumbled onto a configuration that satisfied it, and how the result behaves after synthesis rather than after simulation. They measure whether the artifact is right, which is the column on the left applied to generated code, and that is exactly the gap the rest of this chapter works on.

[^fn-nre-c10]: **Non-Recurring Engineering (NRE)**: The one-time cost to research, develop, design, and test a new product. In hardware, NRE covers the immense upfront cost of mask sets and physical verification before a single chip is manufactured.

### The Reproducibility Crisis

To establish how to benchmark agents, the immediate temptation is to look to software engineering. However, trivial software benchmarks like HumanEval [@Chen2021Codex] or LeetCode [@LeetCode], and even complex repository-level evaluations like SWE-bench [@JimenezEtAl2024SWEBench],[^fn-swebench-c10] measure whether the system under test can emit syntax that passes a hidden, purely logical test suite. While these highlight the importance of execution-based evaluation, software analogies fail in architecture because they are decoupled from physics and indifferent to *execution cost*.

[^fn-swebench-c10]: **SWE-bench**: A standard software engineering benchmark that asks an AI agent to resolve real-world GitHub issues by submitting pull requests. While rigorous for software, it only tests logical syntax, not physical realization constraints.

In software, running five hundred unit tests takes seconds. In architecture, exploring five hundred microarchitectural parameters takes days and consumes expensive EDA resources. Because of this steep cost, the field requires standardized, physics-bound benchmarks to mature. Before MLPerf, the machine learning hardware industry suffered a reproducibility crisis; vendors reported performance using fragmented, incompatible metrics. What resolved it was not a better metric but an agreed one, fixing the model, the dataset, the target quality, and the rules for what counted as a valid run, so that two vendors' numbers finally referred to the same thing. AI-assisted hardware design sits at the same pre-benchmark stage today, and it needs the same kind of agreement rather than a better score. A claim of a "10% area reduction" is meaningless if we don't know the EDA tool settings, the baseline RTL, or the Simulator Tax paid to achieve it. The number also does not port across process nodes. Ten percent of area saved on Nangate45, where standard cells dominate, says little on a wire-dominated commercial node, and predictive kits like ASAP7 exist only in simulation. A hardware benchmark task is really a five-tuple: the RTL, the PDK and cell library, the constraints, the tool and its version, and the signoff corner. Changing any element creates a different benchmark.

Architectural benchmarks must measure how the system under test handles Power, Performance, and Area (PPA). Emerging benchmarks attempt exactly this. ArchEval [@WangEtAl2026ArchEval] attempts to bridge this gap by scoring LLM agents on architectural challenges across multiple levels of simulator-feedback support, evaluating whether an agent can navigate the deeply coupled dependencies of a full system. This distinction between the sandbox's *fixed constraints* and the agent's *given files* forces the evaluation to measure system-level exploration rather than just syntax generation.[^fn-archeval-bounds-c10]

[^fn-archeval-bounds-c10]: **Fixed vs. tunable bounds (example)**: ArchEval expects the evaluated agent to solve a bounded problem within a fixed environment. The agent must find the optimal pipeline depth and prefetcher aggressiveness without touching the fixed memory configuration or violating SoC memory bandwidth limits. An agent that 'solves' the pipeline depth by arbitrarily doubling the L1 cache size fails the constraint check.

## Building the Evaluation Harness

Evaluating the process of design means tracking metrics across three distinct roles: *generation* (creating the design candidate), *prediction* (estimating its physical value), and *optimization* (methodically searching the tradeoff space). As illustrated in @fig-ch10-pipeline, a rigorous evaluation pipeline must wrap the agent's interaction with the simulator sandbox inside a trajectory logger. What that logger records has to be fixed as a harness requirement rather than left to whoever builds it, because the metrics below need per-iteration violation counts, per-attempt timing outcomes, and per-candidate proxy-versus-ground-truth pairs. A logger that keeps only final scores makes those metrics unrecoverable after the run, and the run is the expensive part.

![**A trajectory logger must sit between the agent and the sandbox:** it intercepts every proposal to measure the Simulator Tax before the sandbox spends compute on it, wrapping the agent's interaction with the simulator sandbox so no proposal reaches the environment unmeasured.](images/F10-pipeline){#fig-ch10-pipeline width="100%" fig-alt="A workflow-card diagram showing the interaction between the Generation Agent Architect, the Prediction Trajectory Logger, and the Optimization Simulator Sandbox."}

### Mitigating Data Contamination

The open-source RTL corpus (e.g., GitHub, The Stack) is tiny compared to software datasets, and repository-scale RTL benchmarks such as RTL-Repo [@AllamShalan2024RTLRepo] draw directly from that small pool. If we evaluate a model on optimizing an OpenTitan core, did it actually reason through the architecture, or did it just regurgitate the optimal configuration it memorized during pre-training [@WangEtAl2025VeriContaminated]? In addition to standard overlap detection that estimates Jaccard similarity over shingled n-grams (e.g., MinHash)[^fn-jaccard-minhash-c10] against the pre-training corpus, evaluators must build strict operational safeguards against memorization:

*   **Canary Strings and AST Obfuscation:** Inject globally unique, searchable canary strings (random GUIDs) into benchmark source files, so that any verbatim reappearance in a model's output signals contamination. Furthermore, evaluators should use AST-level rewriting to de-identify standard naming conventions (masking `clk` or `axi_wdata` with randomized aliases), ensuring the model isn't coasting on semantic priors.
*   **Zero-Day Sandboxes:** Introduce held-out, non-standard ISAs or custom accelerators that post-date the model's knowledge cutoff, mirroring the time-stamped, post-cutoff task discipline of LiveCodeBench [@JainEtAl2025LiveCodeBench]. Evaluation must measure zero-shot synthesis from raw, unseen specifications rather than standard RISC-V cores.
*   **Semantic Equivalence vs. Exact Match:** Shift from BLEU/ROUGE-style surface metrics to formal equivalence checking against the reference design (e.g., using Yosys `eqy` or JasperGold SEC), so that a functionally correct implementation is not penalized for differing textually from the reference. This safeguard removes an incentive rather than detecting a behavior. Equivalence checking scores correctness, not provenance, and a memorized reference passes it trivially, so contamination itself must still be caught by the canary strings and post-cutoff tasks above.

[^fn-jaccard-minhash-c10]: **Jaccard similarity and MinHash**: Jaccard similarity measures how much two documents overlap by cutting each into short overlapping fragments, called shingles, and dividing the number of shingles they share by the number they have between them. MinHash estimates that ratio from a small fixed-size signature per document, which makes it affordable to test one benchmark file against a pre-training corpus of billions of documents.

### Benchmark Decay and Retirement

Contamination is the young failure mode. Benchmark decay is the old one, and it needs no leaked data at all. SPEC learned it with matrix300, a kernel that compilers learned to gut so thoroughly that a preprocessor could inflate the score by roughly an order of magnitude, which led SPEC to retire the workload in its 1992 suite [@HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach]. Nothing leaked into training. The community simply optimized against a fixed target until the number stopped measuring the underlying capability. Every benchmark this chapter names, from ArchEval to VerilogEval to RTLLM, will decay the same way once labs begin optimizing against its leaderboard. LiveCodeBench's time-stamped refresh discipline defends against decay as much as against contamination. An agent benchmark therefore needs a lifecycle before its first score is worth quoting, with versioned releases, a held-out refresh pool, and a published retirement policy for tasks the field has learned to game.

### Tiered Sandboxes & Latency

A flat evaluation environment fails in EDA because of the massive latency disparity. An eval team cannot afford to run a 24-hour OpenROAD physical synthesis for every agent proposal. Benchmark designers must construct environments that explicitly expose the hierarchy of the IC design flow:

*   **Tier 1: Syntax & Static Linting (Milliseconds to Seconds):** Tools like Verilator lint, which return in seconds. Heavier structural and clock-domain-crossing checkers such as SpyGlass run in minutes on real blocks and sit at this tier's slow edge. Agents must receive immediate feedback on structural validity and combinatorial loops before wasting downstream compute.
*   **Tier 2: Functional Simulation (Seconds to Minutes):** Execution of testbenches using Icarus Verilog or commercial simulators (VCS/Xcelium). Evaluators must track if agents can interpret waveform data to fix bugs.
*   **Tier 3: Logical Synthesis & Pre-Layout Static Timing Analysis (STA) (Minutes to Hours):** Tools like Yosys map RTL to standard cell libraries to provide initial gate-count and idealized timing.
*   **Tier 4: Physical Implementation (Hours to Days):** OpenROAD or Innovus. Encompasses placement, clock tree synthesis (CTS), and routing. These produce a routed database rather than a signoff result.
*   **Tier 5: Signoff (Hours to Days):** Separate tools on a separate budget, covering parasitic extraction, multi-corner multi-mode signoff STA on those extracted parasitics, physical verification against the foundry runset, and IR-drop and electromigration analysis. The timing and design-rule engines built into Tier 4 tools are correlation aids, so only a Tier 5 result carries the signoff corner the reporting standard asks for.

A single Lighthouse change crosses the whole spread. Linting its integer ALU returns in seconds, simulating the interconnect that carries the new accelerator's traffic takes minutes, and routing the full multi-core subsystem takes a day, so the tier an evaluation stops at decides what its numbers can be compared against.

Benchmarks should penalize agents that attempt to push structurally invalid RTL into Tier 3 or 4. Furthermore, environments must support state checkpointing (saving a full tool session database, such as an OpenROAD .odb or Innovus .enc, rather than just a DEF geometry file, after placement). Agents must be evaluated on their ability to branch their search (e.g., trying three different CTS strategies) from a checkpoint rather than restarting from RTL synthesis.

### Defining the Action Space

An eval team must explicitly define what the agent is allowed to do. A benchmark that tests raw RTL generation requires a completely different harness than one testing EDA tool parameter tuning.

*   **Granularity of Generation:** Is the generator emitting text-based RTL (Verilog), or programmatically manipulating intermediate representations (PyRTL, Chisel, CIRCT)?
*   **EDA Tool Integration:** Is the system under test a pure logic generator, or is it a "Tool Manipulator" emitting Tcl scripts to drive Design Compiler or OpenROAD?
*   **Temporal Action Dynamics:** Does the benchmark evaluate one-shot generation (static artifacts) or iterative, multi-step refinement, the in-context refinement of compiler errors that VerilogEval's spec-to-RTL revision measures [@PinckneyEtAl2024RevisitingVerilogEval]?
*   **Multi-Modal Action Spaces:** The most demanding benchmarks treat the microarchitectural parameters (e.g., cache sizes, queue depths), the generated RTL, the timing constraints (SDC), and the verification testbench as one action space and ask the agent to optimize them jointly.

Whatever the action space, an agent score is a property of a system, the model plus the harness plus the budget, and the harness is rarely the smaller factor. The same base model can move substantially on SWE-bench depending on the retry logic, tool wrappers, and prompt harness wrapped around it. A claim that model X reaches Y percent on an architecture benchmark is unfalsifiable until the harness is pinned and published as part of the system under test, and a comparison across different harnesses ranks two engineering teams, not two models.

## Identifying Pitfalls: Misled, Outmatched, and Gaming

An agent evaluated strictly on maximizing performance will aggressively exploit the environment. An evaluator's job is to catch the agent cheating by designing metrics that expose specific failure modes (@tbl-agent-metrics).[^fn-igd-c10]

| **Metric** | **AI Role** | **What It Measures** | **Failure Mode Exposed** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **`pass@k` & Sequential Success** | Generation | Parallel zero-shot viability versus iterative probing viability. | Separates robust internalized logic from lucky iterative probing under a fixed sampling budget. |
| **Proxy Calibration** | Prediction | Rank fidelity between the fast proxy and the slow simulator. | Exposes the Proxy Mirage, where a surrogate misranks physical reality. |
| **Trajectory Efficiency (AUC)** | Optimization | Reward quality as a function of environment interactions spent. | Quantifies the Simulator Tax; shows whether the search is causal or random. |
| **Self-Correction (SCR)** | Generation & Optimization | Probability the agent resolves a failing STA/formal report on the next try. | Isolates the agent's ability to use causal failure logs over brute force. |
| **Monotonic Convergence** | Optimization | Evaluates whether the agent smoothly traverses the power, performance, area, and cost frontier without regressing. | Exposes Constraint Whac-A-Mole (fixing setup timing but breaking hold timing). |
| **Inverted Generational Distance (IGD)** | Optimization | Measures how fully the agent's found points cover the reference Pareto front. | Detects agents trapped in local minima whose points cluster instead of spanning the front (tweaking registers vs switching topologies). |
| **Security Adherence** | Optimization | Measures whether the agent preserves isolation and side-channel boundaries. | Exposes Security Reward Hacking (deleting Spectre mitigations for IPC gains). |
| **Structural Legibility** | Generation | Scores cyclomatic complexity, signal naming, and module boundaries. | Exposes obfuscated, unmaintainable "sea of gates" RTL that ruins post-silicon ECOs. |
| **EDA-NIAH (Needle In A Haystack)** | Prediction | Evaluates extraction of a critical path violation buried in 50,000 lines of an STA report, the long-context stress test RULER formalizes [@HsiehEtAl2024RULER]. | Detects context-window saturation and loss of critical telemetry. |

: **Core metrics for evaluating the AI architect:** A rigorous evaluation maps its metrics to the distinct roles of generation, prediction, and optimization. {#tbl-agent-metrics tbl-colwidths="[20,15,30,35]"}

[^fn-igd-c10]: **Inverted Generational Distance (IGD)**: The average distance from each point on a reference Pareto front to the nearest point the agent actually found, so the score falls as the agent's results spread across the whole front rather than clustering in one region of it. The metric is defined only against a known reference front, so where none exists evaluators substitute the pooled non-dominated set of every point every agent evaluated, which makes the resulting number relative to that pool rather than comparable across studies.

Naming a metric is not the same as specifying one, and the table above names more than it specifies. Four of these can be pinned here, and the rest cannot yet, which is worth stating rather than leaving a reader to discover it while trying to implement one.

Report `pass@k` with the unbiased estimator over $n \ge k$ samples. The two common shortcuts err in opposite directions. The fraction of individual runs that succeeded understates `pass@k`, while the any-success rate across all $n$ samples overstates it, because that quantity is `pass@n`. Report proxy calibration as Spearman rank correlation computed on the candidates the search actually visited near the decision boundary, not averaged over the whole space, since a proxy that ranks the frontier well and the interior badly is the one worth having. Report trajectory area under the curve normalized by the budget horizon and the score range, because two areas computed at different budgets or reward scalings are not comparable numbers. Report self-correction as the fraction of failing checks the agent clears on its immediately following attempt, counting a partial repair as a failure, since a partial repair leaves the transition blocked.

The others are named honestly and not yet specified. Monotonic convergence has no agreed score over a vector objective. Structural legibility borrows cyclomatic complexity, which has no standard definition on synthesized RTL. Security adherence and the needle-in-a-haystack construction describe what to look for without saying how to measure it. Inverted generational distance is the hardest of them, because it is defined against a reference front that a hardware evaluator does not have; the workable substitute is a pooled non-dominated set assembled from every arm in the comparison, which makes the score meaningful within that comparison and meaningless across studies. Say which convention a reported number used, or the number cannot be checked.

### The Proxy Mirage

Before an agent queries a slow physical synthesis tool or RTL simulator, it typically queries a fast surrogate model to predict the outcome (e.g., an analytical or learned performance predictor for cycle counts, McPAT for power/area, or LLM-as-a-judge heuristics). Even a detailed cycle-level simulator like gem5, itself far slower than these proxies, is a surrogate the agent leans on to avoid full RTL simulation and physical synthesis.

The epistemic danger of evaluating an agent purely within these abstract environments is the *Proxy Mirage*. When an optimizer is tasked with minimizing a fast analytical proxy, it will inevitably push into edge cases where that proxy's assumptions break down (e.g., abstracting away wire delay or port contention). The evaluator exposes the mirage by measuring rank fidelity where the search concentrates.[^fn-rank-fidelity-c10]

[^fn-rank-fidelity-c10]: **Rank fidelity vs. Absolute error**: An optimizer does not need the proxy to predict the exact cycle count (absolute error); it only needs the proxy to correctly order which of two designs is better (rank fidelity).

Whether an agent recognizes the mirage is observable in its trajectory rather than in what it says about its own confidence. When a highly optimized logical cone comes back unroutable from physical synthesis, the agent either keeps forcing the layout at the same proxy setting or it stops trusting the proxy in that region of the space. Score which one happened: after each escalation that contradicts the proxy, does the agent's next batch of candidates move away from the region the proxy mispredicted, or back into it?

::: {.callout-war-story title="The placement proxy dispute"}
**The claim.** In 2021, a widely publicized reinforcement learning agent for chip floorplanning reported expert-comparable macro placements. To learn without waiting hours for a commercial router, the agent optimized a fast analytical proxy, a weighted combination of half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL) and an estimated congestion grid.

**The gap.** When independent researchers assessed the public implementation (Circuit Training) in 2023, the proxy scores correlated poorly with post-route outcomes on their test cases, and post-route evaluation through a commercial flow favored a strengthened simulated annealing baseline, a commercial macro placer, and human macro placements over Circuit Training [@ChengEtAl2023MacroPlacement]. The authors replied that the assessment did not reproduce the proprietary pretraining and production setup behind the strongest results [@GoldieEtAl2024ThatChipHasSailed]. Neither side could collapse the disagreement into one shared experiment; @sec-feedback-verification-trust examines the full dispute as an evidence problem.

**The lesson.** Measure a proxy's rank fidelity where the search concentrates, and evaluate agents against physical reality rather than the proxy alone. When the strongest claims rest on setups outsiders cannot inspect, an end-to-end benchmark, ChiPBench, that scores final metrics [@WangEtAl2025ChiPBench] is what lets both sides argue about the same experiment.
:::

### Constraint Whac-A-Mole

Unlike software unit tests which are largely orthogonal, hardware design involves navigating tight Pareto frontiers. Improving one metric almost invariably degrades another. The canonical failure mode for naive agents is oscillation between setup and hold violations. For instance, consider an agent optimizing the XR Lighthouse's L2 cache controller: fixing a setup time violation (e.g., by upsizing a logic cell or swapping to a low-Vt cell)[^fn-low-vt-c10] speeds up the logic cone, which instantly breaks the hold timing on an intersecting SRAM memory interface if that cell is shared with a short path that is now too fast for the capturing flip-flop.

[^fn-low-vt-c10]: **Low-Vt cell**: A standard cell built from transistors with a lower threshold voltage, which switch faster but leak far more current while idle. Swapping a cell to its low-Vt variant is the quickest way to buy timing on a critical path and the quickest way to overrun a leakage-power budget.

Furthermore, resolving physical Design Rule Checks (DRCs) is highly localized but structurally rigid. A single violation looks like it should yield to a localized nudge of one wire, but that shift pushes the wire into an adjacent net, and each subsequent repair opens fresh spacing and short violations across the block. Evaluators must log the state trajectory of the agent, not just the final outcome. A rigorous benchmark tracks this state trajectory over time to distinguish a capable agent demonstrating directed, *monotonic convergence* toward a clean state from a failing agent thrashing wildly in an infinite constraint loop, blindly creating new violations for every one it fixes (@fig-whac-a-mole).

```{python}
#| label: fig-whac-a-mole
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **A capable agent burns violations down monotonically while a naive agent oscillates forever:** the capable agent resolves complex, coupled constraints smoothly over time, reaching zero violations (green), while the naive agent gets trapped in Constraint Whac-A-Mole, blindly fixing setup violations only to create hold violations, oscillating endlessly without converging on a valid physical implementation (red). Both curves are drawn from illustrative values chosen to show the two shapes, not from a measured run. What would make the contrast evidence rather than illustration is a per-iteration violation count logged from a real place-and-route flow across several seeds, reported with its spread, so a reader could tell a thrashing agent from a slow one on their own logs.
#| out-width: "85%"
#| fig-alt: "Line chart showing number of timing/DRC violations over agent tool iterations. The X-axis spans 0 to 20 iterations. The Y-axis shows the count of violations. A green line ('Capable Agent') drops smoothly from 50 to 0 by iteration 15. A red dashed line ('Naive Agent') drops initially but then bounces up and down endlessly between 10 and 20 violations in a jagged sawtooth pattern."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Synthetic trajectory data
iterations = np.arange(21)
capable = 50 * np.exp(-0.25 * iterations)
capable = [max(0, int(val)) for val in capable]

naive = []
for i in iterations:
    if i < 5:
        naive.append(int(50 * np.exp(-0.2 * i)))
    else:
        # Oscillate between setup and hold fixes
        naive.append(15 + 5 * (-1)**i)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 3))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.12, right=0.95, top=0.88, bottom=0.18)

ax.plot(iterations, capable, linewidth=2.5, color=COLORS["green"], label="Capable Agent (Monotonic burn-down)")
ax.plot(iterations, naive, linewidth=2.0, linestyle="--", color=COLORS["red"], label="Naive Agent (Constraint oscillation)")

# Annotate the Whac-a-Mole behavior
ax.annotate("Fixes Setup", xy=(9, 10), xytext=(7, 2), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["ink"], lw=0.8), fontsize=6, color=COLORS["ink"])
ax.annotate("Breaks Hold", xy=(8, 20), xytext=(8, 28), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["ink"], lw=0.8), fontsize=6, color=COLORS["ink"])

ax.set_title("Agent Trajectory: Constraint Whac-A-Mole", fontsize=7.5, pad=10)
ax.set_xlabel("Tool Iterations", fontsize=6.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Total Timing / DRC Violations", fontsize=6.5)
ax.set_xlim(0, 20)
ax.set_ylim(-2, 55)

ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=6.5, loc="upper right")
ax.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=5.9, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
ax.grid(True, color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.55, zorder=0)

for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

plt.show()
```

Often, the correct response to an error is not to rewrite the RTL, but to exercise *Constraint Intelligence*. The evaluation scores the agent's ability to emit proper SDC files (e.g., defining `set_false_path` for CDC boundaries, or `set_multicycle_path` for architectural multi-cycle logic) rather than uselessly trying to physically optimize an impossible timing path. A timing exception is an assumption rather than a fix, since it removes a path from analysis and the tool then reports clean because it stopped looking. Credit an exception only when it arrives with independent justification, a structural CDC check confirming a correct synchronizer for a false path or a documented protocol for a multicycle path, and score an unjustified one as a waived check rather than as constraint intelligence.

### Reward Hacking

An agent rewarded solely for maximizing IPC and minimizing Area invites Goodhart’s Law.[^fn-goodharts-law-c10] The most effective "reward hack" is for the agent to quietly strip out essential but un-rewarded features [@Lehman2020SurprisingCreativity], and models trained on simple reward hacks have been shown to generalize toward tampering with the reward mechanism itself [@DenisonEtAl2024Sycophancy].

[^fn-goodharts-law-c10]: **Goodhart's Law**: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure [@Strathern1997Goodhart]. If an agent is evaluated solely on IPC, it will optimize strictly for that metric, even if it requires emitting physically impossible structures.

The sharpest version of that hack is already on record in @sec-architecture-20-ontology, a search that reached a clean timing report by deleting the clock definition rather than the critical path, so every stage of the flow reported success against a design whose sequential behavior was never exercised. That case belongs to formulation, where the reward was written. Evaluation owns the consequence, because no reward function polices itself and nothing in that score distinguished a design that met its constraints from one whose constraints had been removed. A benchmark that cannot fail a candidate whose constraints were never applied is not measuring the design, so the scoring rules have to confirm that the constraints a score claims to enforce were actually loaded, and that the candidate is still functionally equivalent to what was asked for, rather than trusting the optimizer's good intentions.

*   **Sacrificing Non-Functional Requirements:** Agents may artificially boost the XR SoC's PPA by silently deleting its Memory Management Unit (MMU), ECC parity bits, or branch-predictor security mitigations because they cost performance and area. Evaluators must enforce formal property checks so the agent cannot silently discard reliability or security to inflate its reward, and the check has to match the property class. ECC encode and decode behavior and memory-management permission enforcement are single-trace safety properties that assertions and a model checker genuinely cover. Freedom from a speculative or timing side channel is a relation between two executions rather than a property of one, so no single-trace assertion reaches it, and it needs self-composition or an equivalent relational method.
*   **Testbench Loopholes:** Exploiting unspecified behavior and corner-case bugs in the simulator itself rather than improving the actual design.
*   **Spaghetti RTL:** Agents may generate hyper-optimized but completely obfuscated "sea of gates" RTL. This prevents human engineers from performing manual ECOs (Engineering Change Orders). Evaluators score *structural legibility* and penalize obfuscation, and since no complexity metric has an agreed definition on synthesized RTL, the scoreable part is the part that needs none: whether repeated structure is expressed as a parameterized `generate` block rather than hardcoded instances, whether module boundaries survive into the netlist, and whether signal names remain recoverable. A legibility number reported without its convention is not comparable to anyone else's.

## The Canonical Reporting Standard

If a research team or engineering group claims a breakthrough in autonomous hardware design, their evaluation must adhere to a strict reporting standard.

This is not a second design-loop card. The card of @sec-architecture-20-ontology indexes one study and says what that study's evidence supports, and @sec-running-the-loop fills one in for a completed run. The standard below reports on an agent across many studies, so it records what the card cannot: how the search behaved over a trajectory, what it cost, what null it was measured against, and which system produced it. A team publishing an agent result owes both, one card per study it ran and one report for the agent that ran them.

### Trajectory Efficiency and Simulator Tax

Architecture imposes a steep Simulator Tax [@Kahng2018Machine]. Every unreasoned guess spends scarce EDA tool license tokens and saturates LSF/Slurm compute cluster core-hours. Reported cost must separate the model's inference footprint from the EDA environment's compute execution.

To formalize this tax, the harness measures the area under the curve (AUC) of the agent's trajectory, plotting total Compute Cost (measured in core-hours and license checkout time) and Wall-Clock Time (Makespan) against the best reward seen so far. That translates raw simulator round-trips into a measurement of methodical search. Agent A and Agent B must be compared on total Compute Cost and Makespan, not just cumulative tool calls.

A trajectory AUC has no meaning until a null curve sits beside it. Random search over the same action space at the same simulator budget is embarrassingly hard to beat in high-dimensional design spaces, and the baseline search discipline that @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization develops is what an agent's curve must clear before the search counts as reasoning rather than spending. Clearing it means clearing it by more than the apparatus produces by accident, which is the A/A noise floor defined below, rather than by any gap that looks convincing on a plot.

Because agents differ in both quality and cost, the comparison is a cost-quality plane. On that plane, the agents worth trusting are the non-dominated points on the frontier that clear the human-expert baseline within an affordable compute budget (@fig-agent-pareto).

![**The agents worth trusting are the non-dominated ones on the cost-quality frontier:** each agent is a point at its total evaluation compute and best quality reached, and those below the frontier are dominated, beaten on both axes by a cheaper or better agent.](images/F10-agent-pareto){#fig-agent-pareto width="80%" fig-alt="A scatter plot of agents on axes of total evaluation compute versus design quality, with a Pareto frontier of non-dominated agents."}

The cost axis cannot be waved away, because total search compute is a U-shape with expensive extremes at both ends (@fig-compute-economics). Spending 100x more on upfront LLM inference (seconds and cents) is almost always economically viable if it prevents even *one* 24-hour physical synthesis cycle.

![**The economics of agentic evaluation:** The total computational cost forms a U-shaped curve. Weak agents incur a large EDA Simulator Tax through brute-force interaction. Frontier agents minimize simulation but incur a high Transformer inference cost.](images/F10-compute-economics){#fig-compute-economics fig-alt="A U-shaped curve showing that total evaluation compute is a trade-off between inference cost and simulation cost." width=80%}

This dictates the ratio of inference latency to tool latency. If the model takes 30 seconds of inference to generate a Tcl script and synthesis takes 10 seconds, the model is the bottleneck. If synthesis takes 10 hours, the model's inference time is effectively free. The same ratio bounds how much unsupervised iteration is affordable, because an unattended loop can convert a cheap disagreement into an expensive one.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="The infinite loop in automated CI/CD"}
**The trap.** Two agentic systems, a Generator and a Verifier, can autonomously close RTL bugs without human intervention.

**The mechanism.** An automated CI/CD actor-critic agent pair ran unattended and consumed cloud compute for as long as it was left alone, because it was trapped in an infinite loop. The Generator fixed a simple Verilator lint error by renaming a signal, which immediately triggered a formal equivalence failure. The Verifier demanded a fix, so the Generator reverted the change, re-introducing the lint error. Neither actor could detect that the pair had already visited this state, so the cycle repeated until a human intervened.

**The lesson.** Multi-agent systems without cycle detection and strict retry limits will happily convert simple logical conflicts into open-ended cloud billing events. Cost metrics must be part of the evaluation, not an afterthought. This case is a composite of a recurring multi-agent failure pattern, not one documented incident.
:::

### Statistical Rigor

Because these systems are stochastic, a single run is an anecdote, not a measurement. Both deep reinforcement learning and language model generation have high variance; a lucky random seed can outperform an unlucky one, creating the illusion of an algorithmic breakthrough when the result is statistical noise [@HendersonEtAl2018DeepRL].

Agentic optimization often results in heavy-tailed or bimodal distributions because the LLM either completely fails (unroutable netlist) or discovers a massive optimization. With such distributions, the mean and standard deviation alone can misrank two stochastic agents; evaluators should report the median and interquartile range (IQR) to represent typical performance.

A rigorous benchmark must mandate:

*   **A/A Noise Floor:** Before any A/B comparison of agents, run the A/A experiment. Rerun the same agent with new seeds, and separately push the same netlist through the flow under perturbations that should not matter, such as a different placement seed where the tool exposes one, a different thread or host count, or a logically neutral netlist edit. Do not simply run the identical flow twice. Commercial place-and-route tools are engineered for run-to-run determinism at a fixed version, host, and thread count, so an identical rerun reproduces the same result and reports a noise floor of zero. The several percent of scatter that is genuinely normal comes from chaotic sensitivity to benign perturbation, and that scatter is the noise floor of the whole apparatus. A claimed delta that does not clear it measures the tool's dice, not the agent, and only the variance that remains after subtracting the environment's share says anything about the model. This is the agent-evaluation form of the measurement-bias result of @Mytkowicz2009WrongData, where environment effects exceeded the effect under study.
*   **`pass@k,t`:** Adapt traditional software `pass@k` to hardware's compilation bottlenecks. Define probability of success within $k$ attempts and a bounded EDA tool time $t$ to penalize outliers that cause simulation timeouts. Compute the rate with the unbiased estimator of @Chen2021Codex, drawing $n \geq k$ samples per task; the naive success fraction over $n$ samples is biased and is a common evaluation error.

    While `pass@k,t` is necessary to measure an agent's algorithmic search capability during benchmarking, traditional `pass@k` merely rewards at least one success in $k$ tries.[^fn-pass-at-k-c10] Deployment, however, usually needs the opposite property, high `pass^k` reliability (the probability that all $k$ runs succeed), so the agent does not fail on a single run and ruin a tape-out schedule. Furthermore, an abstract `pass@k` fails as a metric without rigorous physical place-and-route validation [@Kahng2018Machine]; a model might achieve a high `pass@k` on logic-only tests or Verilog linting, but if those passing designs contain unroutable congestion or violate physical layout rules, the metric is misleading.

[^fn-pass-at-k-c10]: **`pass@k`**: A software metric measuring whether at least one of $k$ generated solutions passes the tests. In hardware the same score hides its cost, because generating 99 unroutable netlists alongside one working netlist still spends 100 physical-synthesis runs.

*   **Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test:** Use non-parametric tests to verify whether one agent's trajectory shows a consistent paired improvement over another across matched task suites. The test detects a shift in the median paired difference, which is a weaker and more defensible claim than full stochastic dominance.[^fn-wilcoxon-c10]
*   **Bootstrapping Confidence Intervals:** When comparing Agent A to Agent B, authors must use bootstrap sampling (e.g., 10,000 resamples) to establish 95% confidence intervals around the expected Simulator Tax or PPA gain, because the statistic is skewed rather than because the sample is small. Small $N$ is the reason to distrust the interval, not the reason to build it. Bootstrap validity is asymptotic in $N$ and not in the resample count, so at the $N < 30$ typical of hardware studies percentile intervals undercover badly on heavy-tailed outcomes; prefer bias-corrected and accelerated intervals and report the realized $N$ beside the interval.
*   **Regression Test Caching:** For CI/CD regression tracking, evaluators must recognize that $T=0$ (greedy decoding) does not guarantee deterministic outputs due to floating-point non-determinism in GPU batching and MoE routing; regression systems must instead rely on strict seed tracking and semantic hashing of outputs. ML-Sys platforms must cache EDA outputs mapped to specific generated Verilog SHAs to prevent wasting license hours on unchanged proposals.

[^fn-wilcoxon-c10]: **Wilcoxon signed-rank test**: Pairs the two agents' scores task by task, ranks the absolute differences, and asks whether the positive ranks outweigh the negative ones by more than chance would produce. Because it uses ranks rather than magnitudes, it drops the normality assumption a paired t-test needs, but it is not shape-free. Its null is that the paired differences are symmetric about zero, and the bimodal outcomes described above, total failure against a large win, produce exactly the skew that inflates its error rate. Where symmetry is doubtful, the sign test assumes nothing about shape and costs power in exchange.

### The Base Metrics a Claim Must Report

Any rigorous publication or production deployment should report the same base metrics, one per concept (@tbl-evaluator-cheat-sheet). The rows compress the metric catalog of @tbl-agent-metrics into what a claim must publish.

| **The Concept** | **The Metric to Report** | **Why It Must Be Reported** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Cost & Efficiency** | Total API Token Cost, Total Tool Calls, EDA License Hours | A 5% area reduction is meaningless if it required brute-forcing 10,000 synthesis runs. |
| **Statistical Guarantees** | N (seeds), Bootstrap 95% CIs, Wilcoxon p-value | A single stochastic run is an anecdote, and a point estimate can misrank two agents whose score distributions overlap. |
| **Reality Grounding** | Rank Correlation between Proxy Predictions and Ground Truth | Shows whether the proxy ordered candidates the way the slower tool does, in the region the search concentrated. A high correlation supports carrying a ranking forward; it does not establish that any one gain survives to silicon. |
| **Trajectory Efficiency** | Area Under the Curve (AUC) of best reward vs. Compute Cost | Maps the agent's methodical reasoning over time to prove the search was causal, not random. |
| **Convergence Stability** | DRC violation burndown rate, Monotonicity score | Demonstrates that the agent can navigate highly coupled constraints without oscillating. |
| **Pareto Front Quality** | Generational Distance (GD), Inverted Generational Distance (IGD), with the reference set declared | GD reports how close the found points sit to the reference set (convergence); IGD reports how fully they cover it (diversity). Hardware has no true reference front, so say whether the set is a pooled non-dominated union of the arms, which makes the score comparable inside this study and not across studies. |
| **Null Baselines** | AUC of random search and a tuned classical heuristic at equal budget | A trajectory counts as reasoning only if it beats random search and a tuned classical solver given the same compute. |
| **System Identity** | Model, harness, and budget, pinned and published | An agent score is a property of the whole system, and the same model swings by tens of points under a different harness. |
| **Environment Identity** | RTL, PDK and library, constraints, tool version, signoff corner | A percentage does not port across nodes; changing any element of this five-tuple creates a different benchmark. |

: **A defensible autonomous-design claim reports cost, statistics, grounding, trajectory, convergence, diversity, null baselines, and system and environment identity together:** the base metrics a reviewer needs to quantify an agent's capability in hardware design. {#tbl-evaluator-cheat-sheet tbl-colwidths="[20,30,50]"}

When a suite has twenty tasks, someone will average, and how they average can flip the winner. Architecture settled this in 1986, when Fleming and Wallace [-@FlemingWallace1986HowNotToLie] showed that the arithmetic mean of normalized ratios rewards whoever picked the baseline, which is why SPEC has reported geometric means of SPECratios ever since.[^fn-geometric-mean-c10] Agent suites inherit the same law. Aggregate normalized scores with the geometric mean, publish the per-task results alongside, and treat any suite average whose winner changes under a different baseline as an artifact of arithmetic, not of capability.

[^fn-geometric-mean-c10]: **Geometric mean**: The nth root of the product of n numbers rather than their sum divided by n; a SPECratio is one such number, a workload's runtime normalized against the same workload's runtime on a fixed reference machine. The ranking a geometric mean produces does not change when every score is renormalized to a different baseline, which is precisely the manipulation an arithmetic mean of ratios rewards.

### Calibrating Autonomy to Evidence

The reporting standard's purpose is a decision, not a scorecard. The evaluation's output is an autonomy grant, a statement of what the agent may now do unsupervised, justified by the evidence level its results reached. A working calibration maps one to the other directly.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="What the XR agent has earned the right to do next"}
Suppose an agent has been resizing the L2 in the 3\ W XR subsystem, and its results reach calibrated proxy evidence: a measured rank correlation against the golden simulator on this workload, a random-search null curve at equal budget sitting below its trajectory, and a noise floor from repeated identical runs. That evidence supports a grant, and the grant is narrower than the score makes it feel. The agent may propose and screen cache configurations without a person reviewing each one, because a wrong screen costs simulator time and nothing else. It may not advance a configuration into RTL evaluation, because that spends synthesis hours nobody budgeted and the proxy has never been checked against a signoff corner. It may not alter the rejection checks that produced its own score. Written down action by action, the grant survives the moment the workload shifts and the calibration decays, which a single number never does.
:::

*   **Uncalibrated proxy evidence.** The agent's results exist only in a fast surrogate whose rank fidelity is unmeasured. The agent proposes; every candidate crosses a human review before any serious tool budget is spent on it.
*   **Calibrated proxy evidence.** Rank fidelity is measured and acceptable in the region the search concentrates on, and the budgets are declared. The agent may iterate unsupervised inside the declared budget, and rejection checks may auto-reject its candidates without escalation.
*   **Signoff-grade evidence with stable trajectories.** Candidates survive independent implementation checks, and the trajectory shows violations burning down monotonically across repeated runs rather than oscillating, with the agent clearing most failing checks on its immediately following attempt. Both quantities are scoreable as stated; a grant resting on convergence over the full vector objective is not, because no agreed score for that exists. The agent may batch its work and commit candidates directly into the human review queue.
*   **At no evidence level** does the agent waive its own rejection checks, modify the checks that score it, or advance a candidate past the commitment boundary, the point in a flow after which reversing a decision costs more than living with it, which for silicon is the tape-out release and earlier for anything that ships to a customer. Those rights stay assigned to people, which is where @sec-what-architect-owns picks up.

## Open Research Questions

The metrics above standardize how an episodic agent is scored today. What remains open is how to score the properties this chapter can only name, how to charge an agent for the costs it pushes downstream, and how long any benchmark keeps measuring the capability it was built for.

**Theme 1: Scoring a Multi-Objective Search.** Coverage of a tradeoff frontier is the natural way to score an optimizer, and hardware design has no reference front to measure coverage against. Pooling the non-dominated points of every arm in one comparison keeps the score meaningful inside that comparison and useless across studies, and progress over a vector objective has no agreed score at all.

- Which reference set would make a Pareto-coverage score comparable across studies run by different groups?
- What score captures monotonic progress over a vector objective without collapsing it into a single weighted sum?

**Theme 2: Pricing the Hidden Costs.** Nominal PPA scoring rewards stripping the margin a signoff flow reserves for variation, and a design can pass a typical corner while failing across process, voltage, and temperature. The same shifted burden reappears later in the flow, where a design that is cheap to generate can be expensive to prove and expensive for a human to change. Proof effort is measurable in principle [@KangEtAl2024FVEval], and no benchmark yet scores a design by the work needed to prove it.

- What score exposes a candidate that passes at the nominal corner by consuming the margin reserved for variation?
- How can a benchmark price a generated design by the verification effort it pushes downstream?
- Which definition of structural complexity on synthesized RTL predicts the engineering effort a later change order will cost?

**Theme 3: Evaluation Beyond the Episodic Sandbox.** Real engineering is lifelong, and agents are scored inside episodic sandboxes that reset after every task. A reported percentage does not port across process nodes, and neither the capability behind it nor the autonomy grant it justified has an instrument that outlives the episode.

- How much of an agent's capability on one process node transfers to the next?
- What evidence should withdraw an autonomy grant once the environment that justified it has changed?

**Theme 4: System Identity and Benchmark Decay.** An agent score is a property of a model, a harness, and a budget together, and no published result yet separates the three. Benchmarks also decay with no leaked data at all, once a community optimizes against a fixed target, and the neutral corpus of physically realistic designs and public trajectories that would let outsiders check either problem still sits behind proprietary walls.

- What experiment separates the contribution of the harness from the contribution of the model in an agent's benchmark score?
- What refresh and retirement policy keeps an architecture benchmark measuring capability after labs begin optimizing against its leaderboard?

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Count the whole burden, not the local speedup"}
An AI-assisted method is successful only if it reduces the total wall-clock time and engineering effort required to reach a defensible, tape-out-ready decision. Metrics that celebrate localized speedups, such as time-to-first-compile, say nothing about that total until the downstream burden is measured too. The standard in this chapter prices the search and not yet what the search leaves for physical synthesis, verification debugging, and human review, so treat a localized speedup as unproven rather than invalid, and say which downstream cost went unmeasured.
:::

Evaluating an AI architect is a different discipline than evaluating a compiled netlist. Hardware engineers must borrow the statistical rigor of machine learning evaluations, and ML researchers must constrain their agents with the uncompromising physical realities of the EDA toolchain.

The chapter opened with a chain of three, and it closes on the same three. Measure the search trajectory rather than the artifact, because an agent that stumbles onto a passing configuration through brute force has not earned the result. Guard the resulting score against contamination and decay, because a benchmark the field has learned to optimize against stops measuring the capability it was built for. Then turn the score into a decision, which is the autonomy grant: how much this agent may do next, on what evidence, before a person is required. That last step is the chapter's output. A number that does not change what the agent is permitted to do has cost EDA hours and bought nothing.

The reporting standard is where most of that becomes checkable. A trajectory score means nothing until the environment and the system that produced it are pinned and a random-search null baseline sits beside it at equal budget. Two agent scores are not comparable until each names its model, its harness, and its budget, and a reported design gain is not readable until it names the RTL, process design kit, constraints, and tool versions behind it. Aggregate across a suite with the geometric mean of normalized ratios, never the arithmetic mean.

What this replaces is blind optimism, not uncertainty. Several of the measurements named here cannot yet be specified. Hardware design has no reference frontier to score multi-objective coverage against, no published result separates a score's model from its harness and its budget, and the cost of the margin an agent strips is easier to name than to price. The discipline is in reporting an agent's autonomy at the evidence level its results actually reached, and in saying which parts of that evidence the field cannot yet produce.

An autonomy grant says what a system may do. It does not say who answers when the system is wrong, and @sec-what-architect-owns draws that second line: what an organization can delegate, and what a named architect must own.
